title: Jurisdiction and Powers of High Courts

cells: Cases related to enforcement of Fundamental Rights and disputes

blocks.content: The writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32.

rows: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights
Applicable throughout the entire territory of India
Discretionary remedy (High Court may refuse relief)
Guaranteed Fundamental Right (Supreme Court cannot refuse)

items: High Courts can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights, whereas the Supreme Court can issue writs only for Fundamental Rights.
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 extends to both administrative and judicial superintendence over subordinate courts.
The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1956 authorized Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states or Union Territories.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The High Court stands at the apex of the state judicial administration in India.
Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other legal purpose.
The High Court's writ jurisdiction is broader in scope than the Supreme Court's remedy under Article 32.
Under Article 227, High Courts possess supervisory jurisdiction over all subordinate courts and tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction.
As a Court of Record under Article 215, High Court proceedings are recorded as perpetual memory and it holds the power to punish for contempt of court.
